subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the eccentricity, coordinates of foci, length of latus rectum and equations of directrices of the ellipse 9x² + 16y² = 144.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.57 — SAQ chapter 8 Ellipse, answer 58, the first question of the chapter (LEVEL-I). On a ★★★ SSP (Super Scoring) page — book p.49 lists page 57 among 13 SSP pages, and the chapter-section table on the same page ranks chapter 8 Ellipse ★★★ (the printed chapter banner on p.57 itself shows only ★★, which this card follows the p.49 table over, per the chapter-section-rank rule). Printed appearances: AP 17 · TS 16,17,19,20. The mark split 1+1+1+1 IS THE BOOK'S: each of the four results — eccentricity, foci, latus rectum, directrices — carries its own printed '1 Mark' margin tag and its own tick box. The book combines the two directrix equations onto one line with a single ± sign (√7x = ±16 ⇒ √7x ± 16 = 0); the second combined equation should read √7x ∓ 16 = 0 for the two lines to be independently correct, so this card writes the two directrices as two separate equations instead of copying that shorthand. insider_note: All four results use only a, b and e, so get those three numbers right first — a mistake here breaks every one of the four marks, not just one.

steps.label: Write in standard form
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own — every result below reads a and b off this line.
steps.memory_tip: Divide by the number on the right so the equation reads = 1.
lines: Here a² = 16, b² = 9, so a > b —
So a = 4, b = 3, and the centre is (0, 0).
steps.why: Eccentricity, foci, latus rectum and directrices are all read off a² and b² in the standard form x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, and whether a > b shows which axis carries the foci.
common_mistakes: Using 9 and 16 as a² and b² directly, without dividing by 144 first.
Not checking a > b before deciding the ellipse is horizontal.

steps.label: Eccentricity
steps.margin_note: First mark. a = 4, b = 3 from the standard form above.
steps.memory_tip: Bigger squared minus smaller squared, square-rooted, over the bigger axis length.

lines.text: For a horizontal ellipse b² = a²(1 − e²),

steps.why: For a horizontal ellipse (a > b) the eccentricity is the square root of a² − b², divided by a — not by a² — once the root is taken.
common_mistakes: Leaving a² in the denominator instead of a.
Subtracting b² − a² instead of a² − b², which gives a negative number under the root.

steps.label: Foci
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The two 4's in a·e cancel, leaving just √7.
steps.memory_tip: Foci sit on the longer axis, at a distance ae from the centre.

lines.text: The foci are on the x-axis, a distance ae

steps.why: The foci of a horizontal ellipse lie on the major axis, at distance ae from the centre on each side.
common_mistakes: Placing the foci on the y-axis instead of the x-axis for a horizontal ellipse.
Using e alone instead of ae for the distance.

steps.label: Length of latus rectum
steps.margin_note: Third mark. A short formula — do not overthink it.
steps.memory_tip: Latus rectum equals 2 times the smaller square, over the bigger axis length.

lines.text: The latus rectum is the chord through a focus,

steps.why: The latus rectum is the chord through a focus, perpendicular to the major axis; its length depends only on b² and a, never on e directly.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to double b² before dividing by a.

steps.label: Equations of directrices
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Two separate vertical lines, one on each side of the centre.
steps.memory_tip: Foci use a·e (multiply); directrices use a/e (divide).

lines.text: The directrices are perpendicular to the major
Multiply by √7 and bring 16 to the left:

steps.why: Each directrix is the vertical line x = a/e or x = −a/e for a horizontal ellipse — the reciprocal relation of the focus formula x = ±ae.
common_mistakes: Confusing the directrix formula x = a/e with the focus formula x = ae.
Multiplying 4 by √7/4 instead of dividing by it (not turning the fraction upside down), which gives √7 instead of the correct 4 × 4/√7 = 16/√7.
